slides.heading: Parliamentary Procedures and Powers of Parliament
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how Parliament **meets**, **asks questions**, **moves motions** and stops members from **switching sides**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: sessions and quorum, Question Hour and Zero Hour, adjournment and no-confidence motions, and the Anti-Defection Law
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: In the last chapter we met the two Houses of Parliament and their presiding officers. Now we see how Parliament actually works day to day. When does it meet, and how many members must be present? How do members question ministers? Which motions can embarrass or even remove a government? And what stops members from changing parties for personal gain?

slides.heading: Sessions of Parliament
slides.body_md: The **President** summons and prorogues the Houses. Parliament must meet **at least twice a year**, with **no more than six months** between sessions.

slides.narration: Parliament does not sit all year. The President summons each House to a session and later prorogues it, acting on the advice of the government. The Constitution sets two rules: there must be at least two sessions a year, and the gap between one session and the next cannot be more than six months. In practice there are three sessions: Budget, Monsoon and Winter.

slides.heading: Prorogation is not dissolution
bullets: **Adjournment:** a sitting ends; the session continues.
**Prorogation:** the session ends; the House continues.
**Dissolution:** the life of the **Lok Sabha** ends; elections follow. The Rajya Sabha is never dissolved.
slides.narration: Three words are often mixed up. Adjourning ends a day's sitting. Proroguing ends a whole session, but the House lives on and meets again. Dissolution ends the life of the Lok Sabha, and a general election follows. The Rajya Sabha is a permanent House, so it is never dissolved.

slides.heading: Quorum
slides.body_md: Quorum = the minimum attendance for business: **one-tenth of the total membership** of the House.

visual.alt: Table: with 543 members the Lok Sabha quorum is 55; with 245 members the Rajya Sabha quorum is 25
visual.caption: Quorum is one-tenth of the total membership, rounded up to a whole member.

slides.narration: Quorum is the smallest number of members who must be present for a House to do business. It is one-tenth of the House's total membership. With 543 members in the Lok Sabha that comes to 55. If too few members are present, the presiding officer must adjourn or suspend the sitting until the quorum is met. This stops a handful of members from making decisions for everyone.

slides.narration: A normal sitting of the Lok Sabha begins with Question Hour, usually the first hour of the day. Members question ministers about the work of their departments. Right after it comes Zero Hour, when members raise urgent matters. After that the House turns to its listed business: bills, debates and motions.

slides.heading: Three kinds of questions

rows: Less than ten days; urgent matter

visual.alt: Table comparing starred questions (oral answer, supplementaries allowed), unstarred questions (written answer, no supplementaries) and short notice questions (oral answer on an urgent matter with less than ten days notice)

slides.narration: Questions come in three kinds. A starred question, marked with an asterisk, is answered aloud, and members can ask follow-up questions called supplementaries. An unstarred question gets a written answer, with no follow-ups. A short notice question is about an urgent matter and can be asked with less than ten days of notice, for an oral answer.

slides.heading: Zero Hour
slides.body_md: **Zero Hour** follows Question Hour. Members raise **urgent matters** without the usual notice. It grew up as a **practice**; it is **not in the rules** of procedure.
bullets: Strength: urgent problems reach ministers at once.
Weakness: no fixed rules, so it can become disorderly.
slides.narration: Zero Hour is an Indian parliamentary practice. It begins when Question Hour ends, around noon, and members use it to raise urgent public issues that are not on the day's list. Because it is not covered by the rules, it is lively and sometimes noisy, but it lets new problems reach the government quickly.

slides.heading: Two important motions

rows: Test whether the government has the support of the House

visual.alt: Table comparing the adjournment motion and the no-confidence motion by aim, support needed, House and result

slides.narration: A motion is a formal proposal for the House to decide. The adjournment motion sets aside the day's business to discuss one definite and urgent matter; it needs fifty members to support it, and it carries a hint of criticism of the government. The no-confidence motion goes further: it asks whether the government still has the support of the Lok Sabha at all.

slides.heading: How a no-confidence motion works

nodes.label: Notice of motion in the Lok Sabha
If passed: Council of Ministers resigns

visual.alt: Flow of a no-confidence motion: notice in the Lok Sabha, support of 50 members, debate, vote, and resignation of the Council of Ministers if passed
visual.caption: No reason need be stated in the motion.

slides.narration: Notice of a no-confidence motion can be given only in the Lok Sabha. If at least fifty members rise in support, the Speaker admits it; no reasons need to be stated. After a debate on the government's record, the House votes. If the motion is carried, the Prime Minister and the whole Council of Ministers must resign, because they are collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.

slides.heading: The Anti-Defection Law
slides.body_md: Added in **1985** by the **52nd Amendment** as the **Tenth Schedule**.

rows: two-thirds of the legislature party agree to merge with another party
votes or abstains against the party's direction without permission (not condoned)
the party condones the vote within the time allowed
is an independent and joins a party after election
a nominated member joins a party within six months of taking the seat

visual.alt: Table of the Anti-Defection Law: grounds for disqualification on the left and the exceptions on the right, including the two-thirds merger and the six-month rule for nominated members

slides.narration: Before 1985, members often changed parties after elections, sometimes for office or money, and governments fell suddenly. The 52nd Amendment added the Tenth Schedule to stop this. A member is disqualified for giving up party membership, voting against the party's direction without permission, or, as an independent, joining a party. A merger supported by two-thirds of the legislature party is allowed.

slides.heading: How the law has changed
slides.body_md: The **Speaker** (or the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha) decides disqualification; courts can review the decision.

nodes.label: 1992: Supreme Court allows review of the presiding officer's decision
2003: 91st Amendment removes the one-third split exception

visual.alt: Timeline flow of the Anti-Defection Law: 1985 Tenth Schedule added by the 52nd Amendment; 1992 Supreme Court allows judicial review; 2003 the 91st Amendment removes the split exception
visual.caption: Three dates to remember.

slides.narration: Three dates matter. In 1985 the law was added. In 1992 the Supreme Court held that the presiding officer's decision on disqualification can be reviewed by courts. In 2003 the 91st Amendment removed the old exception for a split by one-third of a party, so today only a two-thirds merger is protected.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: who is disqualified?
slides.body_md: Apply the law to three imagined members.
bullets: A nominated member joins a party in her third month → **not** disqualified (within six months).
An elected member resigns from his party → **disqualified** (voluntary defection).
Two-thirds of a small party merge with a larger one → **not** disqualified (merger exception).
Exam habit: give the **rule** behind each answer.

visual.alt: Table of three imagined members and whether each is disqualified: the nominated member joining in month three is not, the member who resigns from his party is, and a two-thirds merger is not

slides.narration: Let us apply the rules. A nominated member may join a party within six months of taking her seat, so joining in the third month is allowed. An elected member who leaves his party of his own will is disqualified. And when two-thirds of a party's members agree to merge with another party, they are protected. In the exam, always give the rule as your reason.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1
bullets: At least **two sessions** a year; gap **not more than six months**; quorum **one-tenth**.
**Starred** (oral, supplementaries), **unstarred** (written), **short notice** (urgent); **Zero Hour** follows.
**Adjournment motion** (urgent matter, 50 members); **no-confidence** (Lok Sabha only; whole ministry resigns).
**Tenth Schedule** (1985): grounds, two-thirds merger, Speaker decides; split exception removed in 2003.

visual.alt: Flow of the tools of parliamentary control from mild to strong: questions, Zero Hour, adjournment motion, cut motions and no-confidence motion
visual.caption: From gentle questioning to removing a government.

slides.narration: To sum up: Parliament meets at least twice a year with no gap over six months, and needs one-tenth of its members present. Questions and Zero Hour keep ministers answerable. The adjournment motion spotlights an urgent matter, and the no-confidence motion can bring down a government. The Anti-Defection Law disqualifies members who switch sides, except in a two-thirds merger.

slides.heading: Exam tips for Part 1
bullets: Write "**one-tenth of the total membership**", not "one-tenth of members present".
Keep **prorogation** and **dissolution** apart.
Do not say an adjournment motion removes the government; only a **no-confidence** motion does.
For defection, the exception today is a **two-thirds merger**; the one-third split was removed in **2003**.
In 3 + 3 + 4 questions, give one clear point per mark and use the terms in bold.
slides.narration: Some common slips. Quorum is one-tenth of the total membership, not of those present. Prorogation ends a session; dissolution ends the Lok Sabha. Only a no-confidence motion can remove the government. And the defection exception today is a two-thirds merger. In structured questions, write one clear point for each mark.

slides.narration: In this part we follow a bill as it becomes a law. We compare the path of an ordinary bill with the stricter path of a Money Bill, see what happens when the two Houses disagree, and then look at all the powers Parliament uses, and the special powers that belong to each House alone.

slides.heading: The journey of an ordinary bill

nodes.label: Second reading: discussion, committee, clause by clause
Third reading: vote on the bill as a whole
Disagreement or six months' delay: joint sitting

visual.alt: Flow of an ordinary bill: first, second and third readings in one House, the same in the other House, then the President's assent; if the Houses disagree or six months pass, a joint sitting
visual.caption: An ordinary bill can begin in either House.

slides.narration: An ordinary bill can begin in either House. At the first reading it is introduced. At the second reading the House discusses it, may send it to a committee, and considers it clause by clause. At the third reading the House votes on it as a whole. The other House then goes through the same readings before the bill goes to the President.

slides.narration: Think about where the detailed work on a bill happens.

slides.heading: When the Houses disagree
slides.body_md: If the second House **rejects** the bill, insists on amendments the first House will not accept, or **does nothing for six months**, the **President** may call a **joint sitting**.
bullets: The **Speaker** presides.
The bill is decided by a **majority of members of both Houses present and voting**.

visual.caption: Why the larger House usually wins a joint vote.

slides.narration: Sometimes the two Houses cannot agree on an ordinary bill. If one House rejects it, or insists on amendments the other will not accept, or simply sits on it for six months, the President may call both Houses to meet together. The Speaker presides, and members of both Houses vote together. Because the Lok Sabha is more than twice as large, its view usually wins.

slides.body_md: Fill in the blank about the joint sitting.
slides.narration: Which presiding officer takes the chair when both Houses sit together?

slides.heading: The President and an ordinary bill
slides.body_md: The President may **assent**, **withhold assent**, or **return** the bill once for reconsideration. If both Houses pass it again, the President **must assent**.

rows: The bill does not become law
If passed again, assent must be given

visual.alt: Table of the President's three choices on an ordinary bill: assent, withhold assent, or return it once for reconsideration, after which assent must be given if it is passed again

slides.narration: When an ordinary bill reaches the President, there are three choices. Assent turns it into an Act. Assent can be withheld. Or the bill can be sent back once, with suggestions, for Parliament to think again. If both Houses pass it a second time, with or without changes, the President must then give assent.

slides.heading: The special path of a Money Bill

nodes.label: Introduced only in the Lok Sabha, on the President's recommendation
Speaker certifies it as a Money Bill
Rajya Sabha returns it within 14 days with recommendations
Lok Sabha accepts or rejects them

visual.alt: Flow of a Money Bill: introduced only in the Lok Sabha on the President's recommendation, certified by the Speaker, passed by the Lok Sabha, returned by the Rajya Sabha within 14 days, recommendations accepted or rejected by the Lok Sabha, then assent
visual.caption: No joint sitting for a Money Bill.

slides.narration: A Money Bill deals with taxes, government borrowing and spending from the Consolidated Fund of India. It can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha, and only on the President's recommendation. The Speaker certifies it as a Money Bill, and that decision is final. After the Lok Sabha passes it, the Rajya Sabha must return it within 14 days. Its suggestions can be accepted or rejected.

slides.heading: Ordinary Bill and Money Bill side by side
columns:
**Ordinary Bill**
- Either House
- Rajya Sabha can amend or reject
- Deadlock: joint sitting
- President may return it once

**Money Bill**
- Lok Sabha only, on the President's recommendation
- Rajya Sabha can only delay 14 days
- No joint sitting
- Not returned by the President

rows: Can only delay 14 days and recommend

visual.alt: Table comparing an ordinary bill and a money bill on where it is introduced, the President's recommendation, the Rajya Sabha's power, deadlocks and the President's role

slides.narration: Put the two side by side. An ordinary bill can start in either House, the Rajya Sabha can change or reject it, and a joint sitting settles deadlocks. A Money Bill must start in the Lok Sabha, the Rajya Sabha can only delay it for fourteen days, there is never a joint sitting, and the President does not send it back.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: two bills in trouble
slides.body_md: Bill A changes income tax rates; Bill B sets up a river-cleaning authority and the Houses disagree on it.
bullets: Step 1 — Classify: Bill A is a **Money Bill**; Bill B is an **ordinary bill**.
Step 2 — Bill A: the Rajya Sabha has 14 days; its suggestions are not binding.
Step 3 — Bill B: the President may call a **joint sitting**; the Speaker presides.
Step 4 — Conclude: no joint sitting is ever needed for Bill A.

visual.alt: Flow of the method for bill problems: classify the bill, apply its procedure, name who decides and state the outcome
visual.caption: Method for bill problems.

slides.narration: With any bill problem, first decide what kind of bill it is. A bill on tax rates is a Money Bill, so the Rajya Sabha can only hold it for fourteen days and the Lok Sabha may ignore its suggestions. A bill setting up an authority is an ordinary bill, so a deadlock goes to a joint sitting chaired by the Speaker.

slides.heading: Six kinds of powers

rows: Laws on the Union and Concurrent Lists; State List in special cases
No tax without its law; passes the budget and demands for grants
Impeachment of the President; removal of judges
Elects the Vice-President; elected members help elect the President
Amends the Constitution, some parts with ratification by half the States

visual.alt: Table of the six kinds of powers of Parliament with an example of each: legislative, financial, judicial, electoral, amending and control over the executive

slides.narration: Parliament has six kinds of powers. It makes laws, controls money, acts as a court when it impeaches the President or removes judges, takes part in elections to high offices, amends the Constitution, and holds the executive to account. Learn one clear example for each kind, because examiners often ask you to explain three or four of them.

slides.heading: Laws on the State List
slides.body_md: Normally the States make these laws, but Parliament can step in.

nodes.label: Rajya Sabha resolution by two-thirds present and voting (Article 249)
Request of two or more States

visual.alt: Flow listing three situations in which Parliament can make laws on State List subjects: a two-thirds Rajya Sabha resolution under Article 249, a national emergency, and a request from two or more States
visual.caption: When Parliament may legislate on the State List.

slides.narration: Subjects in the State List normally belong to the States. Parliament can make laws on them in special situations: when the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution by two-thirds of the members present and voting that it is needed in the national interest, when a national emergency is in force, or when two or more States ask it to.

slides.heading: Quick check: an electoral function
slides.body_md: Which of these is an electoral function of Parliament?
slides.narration: Look for the option in which members of Parliament choose someone for an office.

slides.heading: Financial power and control of the executive
bullets: No tax without a **law of Parliament**; the budget and **demands for grants** need approval.
Committees check accounts and audit reports.
Control through **questions**, **debates**, **cut motions**, **adjournment** and **no-confidence** motions.

visual.alt: Flow of the tools of parliamentary control from mild to strong: questions, Zero Hour, adjournment motion, cut motions and no-confidence motion
visual.caption: From gentle questioning to removing a government.

slides.narration: Parliament is the keeper of the public purse: no tax can be collected without its law, and no money spent without its approval. It also watches the government constantly, through questions, debates, cut motions on budget demands, adjournment motions and, in the end, the no-confidence motion. These tools range from gentle questioning to removing a government.

slides.heading: Exclusive powers of each House

rows: Money Bills begin here; final say on them
Article 249 resolution on a State List subject
Article 312 resolution for a new All India Service
No-confidence motion against the Council of Ministers
Resolution to remove the Vice-President begins here

visual.alt: Table of exclusive powers: the Lok Sabha controls money bills, demands for grants and no-confidence motions; the Rajya Sabha passes resolutions under Articles 249 and 312 and begins the removal of the Vice-President

slides.narration: Some powers belong to one House only. The Lok Sabha controls money: Money Bills start there, it alone votes demands for grants, and only it can pass a no-confidence motion. The Rajya Sabha speaks for the States: only it can pass resolutions under Article two hundred and forty-nine and Article three hundred and twelve, and a resolution to remove the Vice-President must begin there.

slides.heading: Quick check: a Lok Sabha power
slides.body_md: Which power belongs to the Lok Sabha alone?
slides.narration: Think about money, and about which House the government answers to.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: planning a 10-mark answer
slides.body_md: Question: (i) What is a Money Bill? [3] (ii) How is it passed? [3] (iii) Compare the two Houses' powers over it. [4]
bullets: (i) Meaning (taxes, borrowing, Consolidated Fund) + Speaker's final certificate.
(ii) Lok Sabha only, President's recommendation, 14 days, recommendations, deemed passed.
(iii) Lok Sabha final say; Rajya Sabha delay only; no joint sitting; **reason**: direct election and responsibility.
Aim for one point per mark; the reason in (iii) earns the last marks.

visual.alt: Table planning a three-part ten-mark answer on Money Bills with the marks and points for each part

slides.narration: Here is how to plan a ten-mark question in three parts. Give three points for a three-mark part and four for the last part. For part three, do not just list differences; explain why they exist. The Lok Sabha is directly elected and the government answers to it, so it controls money.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2
bullets: Ordinary Bill: three readings in each House; deadlock → **joint sitting** (Speaker presides); President may return once.
Money Bill: **Lok Sabha only**, President's recommendation, **Speaker certifies**, Rajya Sabha **14 days**, no joint sitting.
Powers: legislative, financial, judicial, electoral, amending, control over the executive.
Exclusive: Lok Sabha (money, grants, no-confidence); Rajya Sabha (Articles **249**, **312**, Vice-President's removal begins there).

rows: Can only delay 14 days and recommend

visual.alt: Table comparing an ordinary bill and a money bill on where it is introduced, the President's recommendation, the Rajya Sabha's power, deadlocks and the President's role

slides.narration: To sum up: an ordinary bill passes three readings in each House, and a joint sitting can settle a deadlock. A Money Bill starts only in the Lok Sabha, is certified by the Speaker, and can be held by the Rajya Sabha for just fourteen days. Parliament has six kinds of powers, and each House has a few powers of its own.

slides.heading: Exam tips for Part 2
bullets: Never write that a Money Bill can go to a joint sitting.
The Rajya Sabha's limit on a Money Bill is **14 days**; for an ordinary bill the joint-sitting trigger is **six months**.
The **Speaker** certifies Money Bills and presides over joint sittings.
Articles **249** and **312** need a **two-thirds** majority of members present and voting in the Rajya Sabha.
When asked to "compare", give points for both sides and a reason.
slides.narration: Watch out for these traps. There is no joint sitting for a Money Bill. Fourteen days is the Rajya Sabha's limit on a Money Bill, while six months of inaction can lead to a joint sitting on an ordinary bill. The Speaker certifies Money Bills and chairs joint sittings. And the Rajya Sabha's special resolutions need a two-thirds majority.

sections.heading: 1. Sessions and quorum
sections.body_md:
- The **President** summons and prorogues the Houses and may dissolve the Lok Sabha (on ministerial advice).
- Parliament must meet **at least twice a year**, and **not more than six months** may pass between two sessions.
- Usual sessions: **Budget** (early in the year), **Monsoon** (about July–September), **Winter** (November–December).
- **Adjournment** ends a sitting; **prorogation** ends a session; **dissolution** ends the Lok Sabha's term. The Rajya Sabha is permanent.
- **Quorum:** one-tenth of the total membership of a House, including the presiding officer. Without it the sitting is adjourned or suspended.

key_terms.definition_md: Minimum attendance for a House to transact business: one-tenth of its total membership.
Ending a session of a House by order of the President, without ending the House.

sections.heading: 2. Question Hour and Zero Hour
sections.body_md:
- **Question Hour** is normally the first hour of a sitting; ministers answer questions about their departments.
- **Starred:** oral reply; supplementaries allowed. **Unstarred:** written reply placed on the table; no supplementaries. **Short notice:** urgent public matter; less than ten days' notice; oral reply.
- **Zero Hour** begins after Question Hour (around noon). Members raise urgent issues without the usual notice. It is a **practice**, not part of the rules of procedure.
- Both keep the executive **answerable in public**.

sections.heading: 3. Adjournment motion and no-confidence motion
sections.body_md:
- **Adjournment motion:** sets aside listed business to discuss a **definite matter of urgent public importance**; admitted only if **50 members** support it; used in the Lok Sabha; implies criticism of the government but does not remove it.
- **No-confidence motion:** only in the **Lok Sabha**; needs **50 members**' support to be admitted; no reasons need be given; after debate the House votes.
- If carried, the **Council of Ministers resigns as a body**, because it is **collectively responsible** to the Lok Sabha.

sections.heading: 4. The Anti-Defection Law
sections.body_md:
- **Tenth Schedule**, added by the **52nd Amendment (1985)**.
- **Grounds for disqualification:** giving up party membership voluntarily; voting or abstaining against the party's direction without permission (unless condoned within the time allowed); an independent joining a party; a nominated member joining a party **after six months**.
- **Exception:** merger with another party supported by **two-thirds** of the legislature party. The **91st Amendment (2003)** ended the one-third split exception.
- The **Speaker** or **Chairman** decides; since **1992** the decision can be reviewed by courts.
- **Assessment:** promotes stability and respects the voters' party choice; but limits free voting and strengthens party leaders.

key_terms.definition_md: A legislator leaving or acting against the party on whose ticket he was elected.
The part of the Constitution containing the Anti-Defection Law.

sections.heading: 5. Making laws: Ordinary Bill and Money Bill
sections.body_md:
- **Ordinary Bill:** may begin in either House; **first reading** (introduction), **second reading** (discussion, committee, clause-by-clause), **third reading** (passing as a whole); same in the other House; then assent.
- **Deadlock** (rejection, unacceptable amendments, or six months without action): the President may summon a **joint sitting**; the **Speaker** presides; majority of members of both Houses present and voting decides.
- **President:** may assent, withhold assent, or return once; must assent if passed again.
- **Money Bill:** taxes, borrowing, Consolidated Fund; only in the **Lok Sabha** on the President's recommendation; **Speaker's certificate** is final; Rajya Sabha must return it in **14 days**, with recommendations the Lok Sabha may reject; otherwise deemed passed; no joint sitting.

key_terms.definition_md: A bill dealing only with taxation, borrowing or the Consolidated Fund, as certified by the Speaker.
A meeting of both Houses together to settle a disagreement on an ordinary bill.

nodes.label: Second reading: discussion, committee, clause by clause
Third reading: vote on the bill as a whole
Disagreement or six months' delay: joint sitting

sections.body_md:
- **Legislative:** Union List, Concurrent List, residuary subjects; State List under Article 249, a national emergency, or the request of two or more States.
- **Financial:** no tax without its law; budget and demands for grants.
- **Judicial:** impeachment of the President; removal of judges.
- **Electoral:** elects the Vice-President; elected members join in electing the President.
- **Amending:** most amendments by special majority; some also need ratification by half the States.
- **Control over the executive:** questions, debates, cut motions, adjournment and no-confidence motions.

- **Rajya Sabha alone:** Article 249 and Article 312 resolutions (two-thirds present and voting); removal of the Vice-President begins there.

questions.stem_md: Which authority formally summons each House of Parliament to meet for a session?

options.text_md: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The President of India. The Constitution gives the President the power to summon and prorogue the Houses (on the advice of the Council of Ministers). The Prime Minister advises but does not summon; the Speaker presides over sittings; the Chief Justice has no role here.

questions.stem_md: What is the longest interval the Constitution allows between the last sitting of one session of Parliament and the first sitting of the next?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Six months. Parliament must meet at least twice a year, and the gap between two sessions cannot exceed six months. The other periods are not in the Constitution.

questions.stem_md: The strip shows the sittings planned for an imagined year: a Budget Session from February to March and a Winter Session in November and December, with nothing in between. What is wrong with this plan?

options.text_md: The gap between the two sessions is longer than six months, which the Constitution does not allow
Parliament may not meet in winter
A Budget Session must last at least six months
There is nothing wrong, because two sessions a year are enough in every case

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The gap between the two sessions is longer than six months, which the Constitution does not allow. From the end of March to the start of November is 7 months, more than the six-month limit. Two sessions a year satisfy the minimum number, but not the rule on the gap. Winter sittings are normal, and no session has a fixed minimum length.

questions.stem_md: In the working of either House of Parliament, what does the word quorum refer to?

options.text_md: The number of votes needed to pass a Money Bill
The total strength of the House fixed by the Constitution
The minimum number of members who must be present for the House to transact business
The members who belong to the ruling party

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The minimum number of members who must be present for the House to transact business. Quorum is the minimum attendance needed for a valid sitting: one-tenth of the total membership of the House. It is not a voting majority, the full strength, or a party group.

questions.stem_md: At a sitting of the Lok Sabha with its present membership of 543, only 48 members are in the chamber when the bell rings. What should the presiding officer do?

options.text_md: Continue, because any number of members is enough once the session has begun
Ask the President to dissolve the Lok Sabha
Adjourn or suspend the sitting until at least 55 members are present
Pass only Money Bills until more members arrive

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Adjourn or suspend the sitting until at least 55 members are present. One-tenth of 543 is 55 (rounded up), so 48 members are short of the quorum. Without a quorum the House cannot do business and the presiding officer must adjourn or suspend the sitting. Dissolution and money bills have nothing to do with attendance.

questions.stem_md: By convention Parliament usually meets in three sessions a year: the Budget Session, the ___ Session and the Winter Session.
questions.solution_md: The usual pattern is the Budget Session (early in the year), the Monsoon Session (around July to September) and the Winter Session (November to December).

questions.stem_md: True or false? When the President prorogues the Lok Sabha at the end of a session, the House is dissolved and a general election must follow.
questions.solution_md: **False.** Prorogation only ends a session; the House continues and meets again in the next session. Dissolution, which ends the life of the Lok Sabha and leads to an election, is a separate act.

questions.stem_md: Explain why a minimum attendance rule matters for the decisions of a legislature, and state the quorum fixed for each House of Parliament.
questions.solution_md: One reason, then the one-tenth rule for both Houses.

answer.model_answer_md: It ensures that laws and decisions are not made by a handful of members, so they carry the authority of the House. The quorum is **one-tenth of the total membership** in both the **Lok Sabha** and the **Rajya Sabha**.

marking_scheme.step: One-tenth of total membership in each House

questions.stem_md: At which point of a normal day's sitting of the Lok Sabha is Question Hour usually held?

options.text_md: In the first hour of the sitting
In the last hour of the sitting

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** In the first hour of the sitting. Question Hour normally takes up the first hour of every sitting. It is not kept for the end of the day, a particular weekday or a particular session.

questions.stem_md: Which feature tells a starred question apart from an unstarred question during Question Hour?

options.text_md: A starred question is answered only in writing
A starred question can be asked without any notice
A starred question can be asked only by ministers
A starred question gets an oral reply on the floor, and members may ask supplementary questions

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A starred question gets an oral reply on the floor, and members may ask supplementary questions. Starred questions (marked with an asterisk) are answered orally, and supplementaries can follow. Unstarred questions get written answers with no supplementaries. Questions without the usual notice are short notice questions, and ministers answer rather than ask.

questions.stem_md: Floods have cut off several imagined villages two days before a sitting, and a member wants an oral answer from the minister at once instead of waiting for the usual notice period. Which device suits her best?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A short notice question. A short notice question deals with an urgent matter of public importance and can be asked with less than ten days' notice, for an oral reply. An unstarred question gets only a written reply after the normal notice; a no-confidence motion targets the whole government; a Money Bill is a law on taxes and spending.

questions.stem_md: Which statement about Zero Hour in Parliament is correct?

options.text_md: It follows Question Hour and lets members raise urgent matters; it is a practice, not a rule written in the procedure book
It is the first hour of the sitting, set aside for starred questions
It is laid down in the Constitution as a fundamental duty of members
It is the time when the President addresses both Houses

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** It follows Question Hour and lets members raise urgent matters; it is a practice, not a rule written in the procedure book. Zero Hour begins after Question Hour (around noon) and grew up as a parliamentary practice; it is not provided for in the rules of procedure. The first hour is Question Hour; the Constitution does not mention Zero Hour; the President's address is a separate event.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A member who receives a written reply to an unstarred question may immediately ask supplementary questions on the floor of the House.
questions.solution_md: **False.** Unstarred questions are answered in writing and are not taken up orally, so no supplementary questions arise. Supplementaries are allowed only on starred (oral) questions.

questions.stem_md: Match each parliamentary device with the description of how it is used.

match_right.text_md: Written answer placed on the table
Matters raised after Question Hour without the usual notice
Urgent matter, asked with less than ten days' notice

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Starred: oral answer with supplementaries. Unstarred: written answer. Short notice: urgent, less than ten days' notice. Zero Hour: urgent matters raised after Question Hour.

questions.stem_md: An imagined member asks the railway minister during Question Hour why a new line promised in her district has not begun. Explain how such questioning helps Parliament keep the executive accountable.
questions.solution_md: Public reply on record, and the pressure it creates.

answer.model_answer_md: The minister must reply **publicly** and on record, so the government has to **explain its actions** and delays. Facts brought out in replies can lead to debates and **pressure for corrective action**, which keeps ministers answerable to Parliament.

marking_scheme.step: Leads to pressure or corrective action

questions.stem_md: Give two differences between starred and unstarred questions in the Lok Sabha.
questions.solution_md: Mode of reply; supplementaries.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. A **starred** question is answered **orally** in the House; an **unstarred** one gets a **written** reply.
2. **Supplementary questions** can follow a starred question but **not** an unstarred one.

questions.stem_md: Some observers praise Zero Hour, while others say it can become noisy and disorderly. Give one argument on each side.
questions.solution_md: One merit and one limitation, each with a reason.

answer.model_answer_md:
**For:** it lets members raise **urgent public problems** at once, without waiting for notice, so new issues reach the government quickly.
**Against:** because it has **no fixed rules**, many members speak at the same time and the time can be lost in **disorder**.

questions.stem_md: What is the purpose of moving an adjournment motion in the Lok Sabha?

options.text_md: To end the session of Parliament
To set aside the normal business of the House and discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance
To remove the Speaker from office
To pass the annual budget without debate

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** To set aside the normal business of the House and discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance. An adjournment motion interrupts the listed business so that a definite, urgent matter can be debated. It does not end a session (prorogation), remove the Speaker (a separate resolution) or pass the budget.

questions.stem_md: How many members of the Lok Sabha must support the request before the Speaker allows an adjournment motion to be taken up?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** At least 50. An adjournment motion can be taken up only if at least 50 members rise in its support. The other numbers are not the rule.

questions.stem_md: Why can a no-confidence motion against the Council of Ministers be moved only in the Lok Sabha?

options.text_md: The Rajya Sabha has no members from political parties
The Rajya Sabha meets only during the Budget Session
The President is a member of the Rajya Sabha
The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha. Ministers hold office as long as they have the confidence of the Lok Sabha, the directly elected House, so only the Lok Sabha can withdraw that confidence. The Rajya Sabha has party members and meets in every session, and the President belongs to neither House.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined year, a no-confidence motion against the government is passed by a majority of the Lok Sabha. What follows?

options.text_md: Only the minister who answered the most questions must resign
The Rajya Sabha must vote on the same motion before anything happens
The whole Council of Ministers, headed by the Prime Minister, must resign

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The whole Council of Ministers, headed by the Prime Minister, must resign. Because ministers are collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha, losing its confidence brings down the whole Council of Ministers. A single minister cannot be targeted by this motion, the Rajya Sabha has no role, and the President is not affected.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** If a no-confidence motion is passed in the Lok Sabha, every minister has to leave office together.

**Reason (R):** The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true, and collective responsibility is exactly why the defeat of the government in the Lok Sabha removes all ministers at once.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** An adjournment motion is commonly moved in the Rajya Sabha to censure the government.

**Reason (R):** An adjournment motion draws attention to a definite matter of urgent public importance.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A is false: the adjournment motion, which carries an element of censure of the government, is used in the Lok Sabha, not the Rajya Sabha. R is true: it is moved to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between an adjournment motion and a no-confidence motion with respect to their aim and their effect on the government.
questions.solution_md: Aim and effect of each.

answer.model_answer_md: An **adjournment motion** aims to discuss **one urgent matter**; even if it is carried, the government **stays in office**. A **no-confidence motion** questions the **whole government**; if it is passed, the **Council of Ministers must resign**.

marking_scheme.step: Adjournment motion: one urgent matter, government stays

questions.stem_md: Opposition members in an imagined Lok Sabha believe the government has lost majority support. Describe the procedure they must follow to test this through a no-confidence motion.
questions.solution_md: Notice, support of 50, debate and vote, consequence.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. A member gives **written notice** of the motion; it can be moved **only in the Lok Sabha**.
2. The Speaker admits it if at least **50 members** rise in its support; it need not state any reasons.
3. After a **debate**, the House **votes**; if a majority supports the motion, the **Council of Ministers must resign**.

marking_scheme.step: Debate, vote and resignation if passed

questions.stem_md: The provisions on disqualification of legislators for changing parties were added as the Tenth Schedule by which constitutional amendment?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The 52nd Amendment (1985). The Anti-Defection Law came with the 52nd Amendment in 1985. The 42nd and 44th Amendments dealt with other matters (including emergency provisions), and the 73rd created the panchayati raj framework.

questions.stem_md: An imagined member elected on a party ticket votes against her party's written direction on an important bill, without its permission, and the party does not condone the vote within the time allowed. Under the Anti-Defection Law she may be

options.text_md: asked to contest the next presidential election

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** disqualified from the House. Voting or abstaining against the party's direction without permission, if not condoned within the time allowed, is a ground for disqualification. The law does not impose imprisonment or offer office.

questions.stem_md: An imagined member elected as an independent joins a political party one year after the election. What is the position under the Anti-Defection Law?

options.text_md: He becomes liable to disqualification, because an independent member may not join a party after election
Nothing happens, because independents are outside the law
He must first resign from the party he never belonged to
He automatically becomes the leader of the opposition

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** He becomes liable to disqualification, because an independent member may not join a party after election. An independent member who joins a party after election is disqualified under the Tenth Schedule. The law covers independents too, and joining a party gives no special post.

questions.stem_md: Who decides, in the first instance, whether a member of the Lok Sabha has become disqualified on grounds of defection?

options.text_md: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
The leader of the member's party

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The Speaker of the Lok Sabha. Under the Tenth Schedule, the Speaker (in the Rajya Sabha, the Chairman) decides questions of disqualification for defection; the Supreme Court has held that such decisions are open to judicial review. The President, Election Commission and party leaders do not decide these cases.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Members are not disqualified when at least two-thirds of their legislature party agree to merge with another party.

**Reason (R):** The Anti-Defection Law was added to the Constitution in 1985.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Both are true. Merger with the support of two-thirds of the legislature party is an exception under the Tenth Schedule, and the law dates from 1985; but the date of the law does not explain why mergers are exempt, so R is not the explanation.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Under the present Anti-Defection Law, a group of one-third of a legislature party can split away and escape disqualification.
questions.solution_md: **False.** The 91st Amendment (2003) removed the exception for a split by one-third of the members. Only a merger supported by two-thirds of the legislature party is now protected.

questions.stem_md: State any two grounds on which a member of a House of Parliament can be disqualified under the Anti-Defection Law.
questions.solution_md: Any two correct grounds.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The member **voluntarily gives up membership** of the party on whose ticket he was elected.
2. The member **votes or abstains against the party's direction** without permission, and the act is not condoned within the time allowed. (Also: an independent joining a party.)

questions.stem_md: Explain how the Anti-Defection Law can help keep governments stable, and give one criticism of it.
questions.solution_md: One way it adds stability; one criticism.

answer.model_answer_md: It discourages members from changing sides for **office or money**, so governments are not brought down by sudden **floor-crossing**. **Criticism:** it restricts a member's **freedom to vote by conscience**, because voting against the party whip can cost the seat.

questions.stem_md: Three imagined members act as follows: (a) a nominated member joins a party in the third month after taking her seat; (b) an elected member formally resigns from his party; (c) two-thirds of a small party's members agree to merge with a larger party. State, with reasons, whether each is disqualified.
questions.solution_md: Apply the six-month rule, voluntary resignation and the merger exception.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Not disqualified:** a nominated member may join a party within **six months** of taking her seat.
(b) **Disqualified:** giving up party membership **voluntarily** is defection.
(c) **Not disqualified:** a **merger** backed by **two-thirds** of the legislature party is an exception.

questions.stem_md: In which House can a Money Bill be introduced?

options.text_md: Only at a joint sitting of both Houses

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Only in the Lok Sabha. A Money Bill can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha, on the recommendation of the President. It cannot begin in the Rajya Sabha, and joint sittings are not used for Money Bills.

questions.stem_md: Within how many days must the Rajya Sabha return a Money Bill sent to it by the Lok Sabha?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 14 days. The Rajya Sabha must return a Money Bill within 14 days, with or without recommendations; otherwise it is deemed to have been passed by both Houses.

questions.stem_md: Two imagined members disagree on whether a bill on income tax rates is a Money Bill. Whose decision on this question is final?

options.text_md: The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The Speaker of the Lok Sabha. The Speaker certifies whether a bill is a Money Bill, and that decision is final for the purposes of the Constitution. The Chairman, the Finance Minister and the Attorney General do not decide this.

questions.stem_md: An imagined ordinary bill on forest protection is passed by the Lok Sabha, but the Rajya Sabha rejects it outright. How can the deadlock be resolved under the Constitution?

options.text_md: The bill lapses permanently and can never be brought again
The Supreme Court decides whether the bill should become law
The President may summon a joint sitting of both Houses, presided over by the Speaker
The Rajya Sabha's decision is final because it represents the States

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The President may summon a joint sitting of both Houses, presided over by the Speaker. For an ordinary bill, disagreement between the Houses (rejection, unacceptable amendments, or no action for six months) can be resolved at a joint sitting summoned by the President and presided over by the Speaker. The bill does not lapse for ever, courts do not decide on passing bills, and the Rajya Sabha has no final veto.

questions.stem_md: Which action is open to the President in the case of an ordinary bill but NOT in the case of a Money Bill passed by Parliament?

options.text_md: Returning the bill to Parliament for reconsideration
Allowing the bill to be published in the Gazette after assent

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Returning the bill to Parliament for reconsideration. The President may return an ordinary bill (once) for reconsideration, but a Money Bill, which is introduced on the President's own recommendation, is not returned. Assent, signature and publication apply to both kinds of bill.

questions.stem_md: At which stage of an ordinary bill in a House are its clauses considered one by one and amendments voted on?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The second reading (consideration stage). Clause-by-clause consideration and amendments belong to the second reading. The first reading is introduction; the third reading is a vote on the bill as a whole with only verbal changes; assent comes after both Houses.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the stages of an imagined ordinary bill, introduced in the Lok Sabha, in the order in which they occur.

options.text_md: Vote on the bill as a whole (third reading)
Introduction (first reading) in the Lok Sabha
Passage through the same stages in the Rajya Sabha
General discussion, committee scrutiny and clause-by-clause consideration (second reading)

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (b) → (e) → (a) → (d) → (c). First reading, second reading (discussion, committee, clauses), third reading, the other House, and finally the President's assent.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: A joint sitting of the two Houses of Parliament is presided over by the ___ of the Lok Sabha.
questions.solution_md: The Speaker presides over a joint sitting (the Deputy Speaker in the Speaker's absence).

questions.stem_md: State two ways in which the procedure for a Money Bill differs from that for an ordinary bill.
questions.solution_md: Any two correct differences.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. A Money Bill can be introduced **only in the Lok Sabha** (on the President's recommendation); an ordinary bill can begin in **either House**.
2. The Rajya Sabha can only **delay** a Money Bill for **14 days**; for an ordinary bill a **joint sitting** can settle a disagreement.

questions.stem_md: An imagined ordinary bill passed by the Lok Sabha has been lying with the Rajya Sabha for seven months without being passed or rejected. What can now happen to it, and who decides the outcome?
questions.solution_md: Six-month rule, joint sitting, majority of both Houses.

answer.model_answer_md: Since more than **six months** have passed without action, the **President** may summon a **joint sitting**. The bill is then decided by a **majority of the members of both Houses present and voting**, under the Speaker's chair.

marking_scheme.step: Joint sitting can be summoned by the President
Decided by majority of both Houses together

questions.stem_md: Explain why the Lok Sabha usually prevails when the two Houses vote together at a joint sitting.
questions.solution_md: Rule of the joint vote and the difference in numbers.

answer.model_answer_md: At a joint sitting the bill is decided by a **majority of all members present and voting**. The Lok Sabha has **far more members** (more than twice the Rajya Sabha), so its view usually decides the result.

marking_scheme.step: Majority of both Houses together decides
Lok Sabha has many more members

questions.stem_md: Parliament removes a judge of the Supreme Court by a special majority in each House after an inquiry finds proved misbehaviour. Which category of Parliament's powers does this illustrate?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Judicial powers. Removing judges (like impeaching the President) is part of Parliament's judicial functions. Electing the Vice-President is electoral, approving taxes is financial, and changing the Constitution is amending.

questions.stem_md: Which of these is an electoral function of Parliament?

options.text_md: Members of both Houses elect the Vice-President
Parliament passes a law on the Union List

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Members of both Houses elect the Vice-President. The Vice-President is elected by the members of both Houses, and elected members of Parliament also take part in electing the President. Budgets are financial, law-making on the Union List is legislative, and the debate on the address is a form of control over the executive.

questions.stem_md: An imagined opposition member moves to reduce the amount demanded by a ministry to one rupee, to show disapproval of its policy during the budget debate. Through this step Parliament is mainly
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** controlling the executive. Cut motions on demands for grants are a way of criticising and controlling the executive through finance. They do not amend the Constitution, elect anyone or act judicially.

questions.stem_md: In which situation can Parliament make a law on a subject in the State List?

options.text_md: Whenever the Lok Sabha passes a simple majority resolution
Whenever a Chief Minister writes to the Prime Minister
When the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution, by two-thirds of members present and voting, that it is necessary in the national interest
Only after the Supreme Court approves the subject

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** When the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution, by two-thirds of members present and voting, that it is necessary in the national interest. Under Article 249 the Rajya Sabha can, by a two-thirds majority of members present and voting, authorise Parliament to legislate on a State List subject in the national interest. (Parliament can also do so during a national emergency, or at the request of two or more States.) A Lok Sabha resolution, a letter from a Chief Minister or court approval does not give this power.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The Union government cannot levy or collect a tax unless a law passed by Parliament allows it.
questions.solution_md: **True.** The Constitution provides that no tax can be levied or collected except by authority of law, which gives Parliament control over the Union's finances.

questions.stem_md: Explain the amending power of Parliament, with one example of a type of amendment that needs more than a special majority in Parliament.
questions.solution_md: Meaning of the power plus a ratification example.

answer.model_answer_md: Parliament can **amend the Constitution**, most parts by a **special majority** in each House. Some amendments, such as those affecting the **representation of States** or the **powers of the States**, also need **ratification by at least half of the State legislatures**.

marking_scheme.step: Example needing ratification by half the States

questions.stem_md: Using the working of an imagined Parliament in one session, describe three ways in which it controls the executive.
questions.solution_md: Three distinct methods of control.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Questions and Question Hour** force ministers to explain their actions in public.
2. **Motions**: an **adjournment motion** highlights urgent failures, and a **no-confidence motion** can remove the government.
3. **Financial control**: ministries spend only what Parliament grants, and **cut motions** and debates on demands allow criticism.

questions.stem_md: Parliament is often called the guardian of public money. Give three reasons for this description.
questions.solution_md: Three points on taxes, spending approval and scrutiny.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **No tax** can be imposed or collected without a **law passed by Parliament**.
2. The **annual budget** and every **demand for grants** must be approved before money is spent.
3. Parliament's committees examine accounts and audit reports, so **misuse** of funds can be exposed.

questions.stem_md: Which power belongs to the Rajya Sabha alone?

options.text_md: Moving a no-confidence motion against the Council of Ministers
Passing a resolution that allows Parliament to create a new All India Service

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Passing a resolution that allows Parliament to create a new All India Service. Under Article 312 only the Rajya Sabha can, by a two-thirds majority of members present and voting, declare that a new All India Service should be created. No-confidence motions, Money Bills and demands for grants belong to the Lok Sabha.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is an exclusive power of the Lok Sabha?

options.text_md: Initiating the removal of the Vice-President
Authorising Parliament to legislate on a State List subject

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Voting on demands for grants. Demands for grants are voted only by the Lok Sabha. Removal of the Vice-President begins in the Rajya Sabha, and resolutions under Articles 249 and 312 are passed by the Rajya Sabha.

questions.stem_md: Why is the Rajya Sabha given a special role when a resolution to remove the Vice-President is to be moved?

options.text_md: The Lok Sabha has no say at all in the removal
The Vice-President is elected only by the Rajya Sabha
The Vice-President is the ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, so the resolution must begin there
The Rajya Sabha controls the finances of the Union

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The Vice-President is the ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, so the resolution must begin there. As the ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, the Vice-President is removed by a resolution of the Rajya Sabha passed by a majority of all its members, agreed to by the Lok Sabha. So the Lok Sabha does have a say; both Houses elect the Vice-President; and financial control lies mainly with the Lok Sabha.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Lok Sabha has the final say over Money Bills.

**Reason (R):** The Lok Sabha is directly elected by the people, and the government is answerable to it.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true, and the direct mandate of the people, with the government's responsibility to the Lok Sabha, is why the Constitution gives it the last word on taxing and spending.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Rajya Sabha can authorise Parliament to make a law on a subject in the State List.

**Reason (R):** Such a resolution of the Rajya Sabha needs a simple majority of members present and voting.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A is true under Article 249. R is false: the resolution needs a two-thirds majority of the members present and voting.

questions.stem_md: Name two exclusive powers of the Rajya Sabha.
questions.solution_md: Articles 249 and 312 (the Vice-President's removal beginning in the Rajya Sabha is also accepted).

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Authorising Parliament, by a **two-thirds** resolution, to legislate on a **State List** subject in the national interest (Article 249).
2. Authorising the creation of a **new All India Service** by a two-thirds resolution (Article 312).

questions.stem_md: Give three reasons why the Lok Sabha is regarded as more powerful than the Rajya Sabha in financial matters.
questions.solution_md: Introduction, limited delay, voting on grants.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Money Bills can be **introduced only in the Lok Sabha**.
2. The Rajya Sabha can only **delay** them for **14 days**, and the Lok Sabha may reject its recommendations.
3. **Demands for grants** are voted only by the Lok Sabha, to which the government is **responsible**.

marking_scheme.step: Rajya Sabha can only delay 14 days
Demands for grants voted by Lok Sabha

questions.stem_md:
An imagined Parliament meets in February. Read the situations and answer.

(i) Explain the constitutional rule about the gap between sessions and name the three sessions usually held in a year. **[3]**
(ii) What is meant by quorum? What must the presiding officer do if the quorum is not present? **[3]**
(iii) Describe how Question Hour works, distinguishing the types of questions, and say how Zero Hour differs from it. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Gap rule and sessions; quorum and its effect; question types and Zero Hour.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Parliament must meet **at least twice a year**, and **not more than six months** may pass between two sessions. The usual sessions are the **Budget**, **Monsoon** and **Winter** Sessions.

(ii) **Quorum** is the minimum number of members who must be present for the House to do business: **one-tenth of its total membership**. If it is lacking, the presiding officer **adjourns or suspends** the sitting until it is met.

(iii) **Question Hour** is the **first hour** of a sitting. **Starred** questions get **oral** answers with **supplementaries**; **unstarred** questions get **written** answers; **short notice** questions on urgent matters may be asked with **less than ten days' notice**. **Zero Hour** follows Question Hour; members raise urgent issues without the usual notice, and it is a **practice** not found in the rules.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about motions in the Lok Sabha.

(i) What is an adjournment motion? State the support it needs and one way it helps the opposition. **[3]**
(ii) Explain the procedure for a no-confidence motion. **[3]**
(iii) Why does the defeat of the government on a no-confidence motion lead to the resignation of all ministers? Explain with reference to the principle involved. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Adjournment motion; no-confidence procedure; collective responsibility.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) A motion to **set aside the normal business** to discuss a **definite matter of urgent public importance**. It needs the support of at least **50 members**. It lets the opposition draw immediate attention to a **government failure**, since it carries an element of **censure**.

(ii) Notice of the motion is given in the **Lok Sabha** only; the Speaker admits it if **50 members** support it; it need **not state reasons**; after a **debate** the House **votes**.

(iii) Ministers are **collectively responsible** to the Lok Sabha: they stand or fall **together**. A successful no-confidence motion shows that the government has **lost the confidence of the House**, so the **Prime Minister and the whole Council of Ministers** must resign; this keeps the executive **answerable** to the elected House.

marking_scheme.step: (iii) Whole Council resigns and why it matters

questions.stem_md:
The Anti-Defection Law changed how members of Parliament behave.

(i) When and by which amendment was it added to the Constitution, and in which Schedule is it found? **[3]**
(ii) State three grounds on which a member can be disqualified. **[3]**
(iii) Who decides questions of disqualification? Evaluate the law by giving two of its benefits and two of its limitations. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Origin; grounds; deciding authority and a balanced evaluation.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) It was added in **1985** by the **52nd Amendment** as the **Tenth Schedule** of the Constitution.

(ii) A member is disqualified if he **voluntarily gives up** his party membership; if he **votes or abstains against the party's direction** without permission (not condoned within the time allowed); or, being an **independent**, joins a party after election (a **nominated** member may join only within six months).

(iii) The **Speaker** (or the **Chairman** in the Rajya Sabha) decides, subject to **judicial review**. **Benefits:** it curbs **floor-crossing** for office or money and gives governments **stability**. **Limitations:** it restricts a member's **freedom of conscience** and strengthens **party bosses**, and decisions by presiding officers have sometimes been **delayed** or questioned.

marking_scheme.step: (iii) Speaker or Chairman decides, with review

questions.stem_md:
Trace an imagined ordinary bill on road safety from its introduction to its becoming law.

(i) Describe the three readings of the bill in the House where it is introduced. **[3]**
(ii) What can the second House do with the bill? **[3]**
(iii) Explain how a disagreement between the Houses is settled, and the choices before the President when the bill reaches him. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Readings; second House options; joint sitting and assent.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **First reading:** the bill is **introduced** and published. **Second reading:** general discussion, possible reference to a **committee**, and **clause-by-clause** consideration with amendments. **Third reading:** the House votes on the bill **as a whole**.

(ii) The other House goes through the same stages. It may **pass** the bill, pass it **with amendments**, **reject** it, or **take no action**.

(iii) If the Houses disagree, or **six months** pass without action, the **President** may summon a **joint sitting**, presided over by the **Speaker**; the bill is decided by a **majority of members of both Houses present and voting**. The President may then **give assent**, **withhold** it, or **return** the bill once for reconsideration; if both Houses pass it again, the President **must assent**.

marking_scheme.step: (ii) Four options of the second House

questions.stem_md:
Money Bills follow a special path in Parliament.

(i) What is a Money Bill and who decides whether a bill is one? **[3]**
(ii) Describe the procedure for passing a Money Bill. **[3]**
(iii) Compare the powers of the two Houses over Money Bills and explain why the difference exists. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Meaning and certification; procedure; comparison and reason.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) A **Money Bill** deals only with matters such as **taxes**, **borrowing** by the government and spending from the **Consolidated Fund**. The **Speaker** of the Lok Sabha certifies a Money Bill, and the decision is **final**.

(ii) It is introduced **only in the Lok Sabha** on the **President's recommendation**. After the Lok Sabha passes it, the **Rajya Sabha** must return it within **14 days**, with or without recommendations; the Lok Sabha may **accept or reject** them; if not returned in time, the bill is **deemed passed**; then it goes for **assent**.

(iii) The **Lok Sabha** has the **final say**, while the **Rajya Sabha** can only **delay** for 14 days and **recommend**; there is **no joint sitting**. The difference exists because the Lok Sabha is **directly elected** and the government is **responsible** to it, so control of the public purse rests with the people's House.

questions.stem_md:
Parliament is the supreme law-making body of the Union.

(i) Explain the legislative powers of Parliament, including two situations in which it can make laws on State List subjects. **[3]**
(ii) Explain any three of its judicial and electoral functions. **[3]**
(iii) Describe Parliament's financial powers and its amending power. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Legislative; judicial and electoral; financial and amending.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Parliament makes laws on the **Union List**, the **Concurrent List** and **residuary** subjects. It can legislate on **State List** subjects when the **Rajya Sabha** passes a **two-thirds** resolution in the national interest, or during a **national emergency** (also at the request of two or more States).

(ii) **Judicial:** it can **impeach the President** and **remove judges** of the Supreme Court and High Courts. **Electoral:** members of both Houses elect the **Vice-President**, and elected members take part in electing the **President**.

(iii) **Financial:** no tax can be levied without a **law of Parliament**; it passes the **budget**, votes **demands for grants** and checks spending through its committees. **Amending:** it can **amend the Constitution**, mostly by a **special majority**; some amendments also need **ratification by half the States**.

questions.stem_md:
The two Houses of Parliament are not equal in every respect.

(i) State three exclusive powers of the Lok Sabha. **[3]**
(ii) State three exclusive powers or special roles of the Rajya Sabha. **[3]**
(iii) "The Rajya Sabha is not merely a delaying chamber." Do you agree? Give reasons for your answer, considering both sides. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Lok Sabha powers; Rajya Sabha powers; a balanced judgement.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Money Bills can be **introduced only in the Lok Sabha**; **demands for grants** are voted only by it; and the Council of Ministers is **responsible** to it, so only it can pass a **no-confidence motion**.

(ii) The Rajya Sabha alone can authorise Parliament to legislate on a **State List** subject (two-thirds resolution, **Article 249**); it alone can authorise a **new All India Service** (**Article 312**); and a resolution to **remove the Vice-President** must begin in it.

(iii) **Yes, partly:** it **revises** ordinary bills, can **reject** them, has **equal power** on constitutional amendments, and protects the **interests of the States** through its special resolutions. **But** on **Money Bills** it can only **delay for 14 days**, and at a **joint sitting** the larger Lok Sabha usually prevails. So it is a **revising and federal chamber**, weaker than the Lok Sabha in finance.

questions.stem_md:
In the parliamentary system the executive is answerable to the legislature.

(i) Explain how Question Hour and Zero Hour help Parliament control the executive. **[3]**
(ii) How do the adjournment motion and the no-confidence motion add to this control? **[3]**
(iii) Some argue that a government with a large majority faces little real control from Parliament. Evaluate this view. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Questions and Zero Hour; motions; balanced evaluation.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) In **Question Hour** ministers must **answer questions** in public, on record; starred questions allow **supplementaries** that probe further. In **Zero Hour** members raise **urgent public issues** without notice, bringing them quickly to the government's attention.

(ii) An **adjournment motion** forces a debate on a **definite urgent matter** and implies **censure**. A **no-confidence motion** tests whether the government still has a **majority**; if it is passed, the **whole Council of Ministers** resigns.

(iii) **For the view:** with a big majority, a **no-confidence motion** is unlikely to succeed and **party discipline** (backed by the **Anti-Defection Law**) limits dissent. **Against:** **questions**, **debates**, **committees** and the **budget process** still expose failures to the **public and the media**, and the government must face the voters at the **next election**. So control remains, though mostly through **accountability and publicity** rather than defeat.
